passage:
Kashish,
I'm writing this because I can't say it properly out loud. I'm sorry for Saturday. When you asked if I wanted to come to the fair, I snapped "Stop asking me stuff!" and slammed the door. You didn't deserve that.
I don't even know why I was angry. One minute I was fine and then everything felt too loud. It keeps happening this year. Mummy says a lot of it is growing up, and to talk to the doctor if it gets too much, which I might.
What I'm trying now is to say "give me ten minutes" instead of snapping. It worked twice this week.
Can we go to the fair next week instead? I'll buy the candyfloss.
Nikita

qa.q: What did Nikita snap at Kashish?
qa.a: Nikita snapped "Stop asking me stuff!" and slammed the door.

qa.q: What does Nikita mean by "everything felt too loud"?
qa.a: Nikita is describing a sudden wave of irritation that came unchosen and can't be fully explained, which is confusing.

qa.q: Why is saying "give me ten minutes" a good step for Nikita?
qa.a: It gives Nikita space to let the mood pass without hurting someone, and tells others what is needed.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Kashish will probably feel relieved and understood, knowing the snap wasn't really about Kashish, and happy about the fair plan. 🤍

grounding: A teen writes an apology showing an understanding of sudden moods and choosing a better way to act.

passage: You're recording? Okay. I'm Kunal. I used to think I was just an angry person. Like, this year my younger cousin Bhupen came to stay, and he's nice, but everything he did annoyed me. The way he chewed. The way he said "bro." I'd feel this heat rising and I'd say something mean. Then later I'd feel awful and not know why I said it. My dad said he was the same at my age and that the moods pass, but I still have to choose what I do. So now when the heat comes, I go to the terrace for a bit. Sometimes I put on music. Bhupen and I actually play carrom now. I still get annoyed by the chewing though. That hasn't changed.

qa.q: Where does Kunal go when the heat rises?
qa.a: Kunal goes to the terrace for a bit.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel after saying something mean to Bhupen?
qa.a: Kunal felt awful and confused about the mean words, which shows the anger didn't match Kunal's real feelings about Bhupen.

qa.q: Why is going to the terrace a useful habit for Kunal?
qa.a: It gives Kunal a pause between the feeling and the action, so the mood can pass without Kunal hurting Bhupen.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have seen Kunal before the change?
qa.a: He probably felt unwelcome and confused, not knowing why his cousin kept snapping at small things like chewing.

grounding: A teen describes sudden irritability and choosing to step away rather than lash out.

passage: My brother Varun turned fifteen in March, and since then I've been living with a weather forecast I can't read. I'm Kavitha, his older sister. Some evenings he tells us jokes at dinner. Other evenings he slams his plate down because the rice is "too wet." Last Tuesday, Mummy asked about his homework, and he shouted. Then, a minute later, he came back from his room. His ears were red. "Sorry," he mumbled. "I'm just... I don't know." He went to fill the water bottles, which is his job, without being asked. I don't know what goes on in his head. But I've noticed he comes back faster now. Mummy says to give him room and not tease. I'm trying, though it's hard.

qa.q: What did Varun complain about the rice?
qa.a: He said it was "too wet."

qa.q: What might Varun's red ears suggest when he came back?
qa.a: They suggest he felt embarrassed and sorry about shouting, even though he couldn't explain his mood.

qa.q: How could the family support Varun during his mood swings?
qa.a: They could give him space in the moment, as Mummy says, and notice when he chooses to come back and repair things.

qa.q: What is it like for Kavitha to live with Varun's changing moods?
qa.a: It feels unpredictable and sometimes hard, but she's trying to be patient and notices small improvements.

grounding: A sister observes a teen's sudden irritability and his growing choice to return and repair.

passage: Monday: Sudha, fourteen, came home and her little sister Damini asked to borrow her pencil box. 'Why do you always TAKE my things?' Sudha shouted, and slammed the door. Later she felt awful and didn't know why she had exploded. Thursday: Sudha started a note on her phone: 'Moods.' She wrote down when she'd snapped. Hungry after school. Tired. Too many tests. She noticed it came in waves, often from nowhere. Mummy said her body was changing a lot and it was common, but she could still choose what to do. The next Tuesday: Damini peeked in. Sudha felt the heat rise. 'Dami, I'm in a mood. Give me ten minutes. Not about you.' After a snack, she called Damini back to play ludo.

qa.q: What did Damini ask to borrow on Monday?
qa.a: Sudha's pencil box.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel after slamming the door on Monday?
qa.a: She felt awful and confused about why she had exploded over something small.

qa.q: What did Sudha do on Tuesday that could help other teens with sudden moods?
qa.a: She named her mood, asked for a short break and explained it wasn't the other person's fault.

qa.q: How might Damini experience the difference between Monday and Tuesday?
qa.a: On Monday she felt shouted at for nothing, but on Tuesday she knew it wasn't about her and got to play later. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teen noticing sudden irritable moods and choosing how to act despite them.

passage: Jeevan, you slammed your door three times this week. No, I'm not scolding. I'll tell you about me at fourteen. One minute I'd be laughing with my friends, and the next I'd want to throw my books out of the window. I once shouted at my father because the dal was too salty, then cried in the bathroom, not knowing why. My mother said, 'Rashmi, your body is changing, the storms will come. You can't stop the rain, but you can hold the umbrella.' She taught me to go for a walk around the building before saying anything. It didn't always work. But more often, by the end of the walk, the storm had passed. Want to walk with me now?

qa.q: What did young Rashmi shout at her father about?
qa.a: That the dal was too salty.

qa.q: How did young Rashmi feel after shouting at her father?
qa.a: She felt confused and upset, crying in the bathroom without knowing why.

qa.q: What does Rashmi suggest Jeevan try when a mood hits?
qa.a: Walking around the building before saying anything, to let the storm pass.

qa.q: What might Jeevan feel when Rashmi says this is not a scolding?
qa.a: Jeevan might feel relieved and understood, and more willing to talk about those moods.

grounding: An elder recalls teenage mood shifts and a strategy for choosing how to act despite them.
